HEADLINE: The (superior) sound of silence
TEXT:
Here’s a guessing game for you. Which man of power wrote these three tweets?

“Trump blames me for WSJ poll, fights FoxNews. Time to calm down. If I running anti-Trump conspiracy then doing lousy job!” “Hillary speech awful point after point.

Eg, better education but against charters, rein in Wall St which she will never do, etc.”

“Life changing innovation 20th cent first Wright Bros, last the Internet. 21st cent?

Smart phones, search, social media. All shrinking world” To the untrained eye, they look like the ramblings of an illiterate five-year-old. Yet each one of them is the handiwork of a man widely considered one of the most powerful in the world. Take a bow Rupert Murdoch: exhibit A in the argument that possessing power is all about mystique – and the careful cultivation of it.

Social media is, by and large, the enemy of the powerful. Or at least, it’s the enemy of the powerful who mistakenly believe trying to tap into the zeitgeist by setting up an Instagram account is a really cool idea.

Sure, Malcolm Turnbull helped mitigate his Prince of Point Piper tag in the early days by posting pictures of himself on trains and buses. But did anyone seriously forget that he had enough money to get about in a private jet, should he choose?

And yes, NSW Premier Mike Baird does a good line in self-deprecation. His tweets about watching The Bachelor with his daughters were amusing, and he cannily cast the news that he’d fallen down the stairs in the middle of the night and fractured his vertebrae as a silly duffer moment rather than cause for concern.

But did we really need to know that he wears socks to bed? And given that once lodged in the mind such a graphic visual is hard to unsee, did it enhance his image?

The answer is no, and no. To my mind, not a single present-day person of power and prestige has had their reputation enhanced by letting the world see how limited their thought processes are – or how daggy their home life. Politicians may rabbit on about the facility of speaking directly to constituents without the filter of some pesky newspaper or TV journalist, but no-one believes for a second that that’s why they tweet.

Social media is all about affirmation.

And say what you like about its imagerefining and marketing attributes, those who do a lot of it, nay, who get addicted to it, have a grasping need to be liked.

Literally and Facebook-figuratively. Come to think of it, that makes it the perfect medium for politicians.

But only the needy ones. Consider Genghis Khan, Mao Zedong, Joseph Stalin and Attila the Hun. Now there was real power. And not a tweeter among them.

Would Machiavelli have maintained a Snapchat account? Good god no. Would Margaret Thatcher have passed the poll tax if she’d been fussing over her status update?

Of course not. The lady would not have been for tweeting.

Cast your eye over this magazine’s covert power list. How many tweets do you suppose Martin Parkinson, Bruce McWilliam or David Gonski have sent between them? None. Zero. Zip.

They understand the importance of silence.

They appreciate the tactical advantage that comes from not telegraphing your every waking thought. They recognise that even they are prone to the occasional brain lapse – but why share it with the world?

During a speaking engagement in Brisbane earlier this year, former prime minister John Howard – who arguably knows a thing or two about power – said he had nothing but contempt for the fatuousness of Facebook and Twitter.

“Facebook is for the impetuous,” he said.

“Developing inadequacies and foolishness into an art form.”

#wisewords. ●

HEADLINE: SECTORAL
TEXT:
Deals

Words ● ANTHONY MACDONALD AND SARAH THOMPSON

It’s been a tough year for dealmakers. Their big clients have reined in growth. Banks and other top 50 companies are shedding difficult assets and shoring up capital positions. Top-tier miners are focused on debt and dividends, while debt markets make it almost impossible for multibillion-dollar leveraged buyouts.

It’s the type of year in which rainmakers are involved in the major corporate restructures, stay close to governments pursuing privatisations and work quietly with their blue-chip corporate clients, many of whom have had changes at the chief executive level in the past 18 months. There will come a time when these new management teams are ready to think about growth, and the rainmakers want to be a part of it.

It feels like the darkness before dawn. As the list of top 50 companies threatens to change quickly, so too will the rainmakers. Rising stars are jostling for power, while second-tier banks and the boutiques are seeking to make up ground on the leaders. Goldman Sachs, Macquarie Capital and UBS, with the biggest teams in the market, are fighting to stay at the top.

Former UBS banker Michael Stock, hired to run Credit Suisse’s investment bank this year, showed it is possible to take an enviable list of clients from the UBS machine to another fi rm. It’s already paid off for Credit Suisse and Stock – the Swiss bank is leading the pack of chasers for the first time in years.

01. Robin Bishop

The Macquarie Capital head is arguably the best execution banker in the market. He gets Macquarie on deals where his rivals fail and always drives his team with the mantra “what can we do better”. Bishop has the benefi t of running Australia’s biggest investment bank, but has an unparalleled ability to marshal the power of the Macquarie machine. He has immediate access to his chief executive Nicholas Moore and the keys to the group’s sizeable balance sheet.

02. Christian Johnston

Goldman Sachs is the No.1 brand in mergers globally and local investment banking boss Johnston expects no less in the Australian market. He is regarded as one of Australia’s best M&A strategists and fi ercest competitors. He advised Asciano through its $9 billion bidding war, which saw it split between an impressive list of heavyweight investors, and has spent a lot of time with Oil Search in the past year.

03. Richard Wagner

Morgan Stanley’s head of investment banking is a first point of contact for governments considering utilities and infrastructure privatisations, and big global investors seeking deals in the sector. Wagner’s reach has gone further in recent years, taking his team outside his utilities and infrastructure patch with work for the likes of James Packer’s Consolidated Press Holdings and Woolworths in the past 12 months.

04. Matthew Grounds

UBS is developing its next tier of bankers in the expectation that chief Grounds will step away at some point. But while he remains at the helm, rightly or wrongly he will be credited for a lot of the bank’s ongoing success. Grounds is supported by a strong bench of M&A and capital markets bankers who do the heavy lifting. Capital markets head Robbie Vanderzeil, utilities banker Jarrod Key and the real estate team are well regarded by their peers.

05. Aidan Allen

One of the hardest jobs in investment banking over the past 20 years has been turning around the fortunes of Citigroup.

But Allen’s move to Citi from UBS in 2013 may not necessarily have been foolhardy. He’s taken on the job of head of investment banking with trademark self-confidence and shown his ability to hustle. Key clients include Woolworths, Qantas, Pacific Equity Partners and Bain Capital.

TechnologyWords ● PAUL SMITH

In the lead-up to Christmas 2015, the local tech scene seemed more powerful than it had ever been. You couldn’t read a newspaper without seeing pictures of Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull or his fresh-faced assistant minister for innovation, Wyatt Roy, visiting a start-up co-working space and championing the “ideas boom” as the future of the Australian economy.

By the time the election came around in July, however, the National Innovation and Science Agenda had moved somewhat into the shadows, as political strategists deemed the electorate unready to fully embrace the tech-led future.

But disruption is here to stay and the investors and entrepreneurs in the vanguard of the digital economy are increasingly mainstream figures who wield significant influence both economically and politically as they seek to position Australia as an attractive tech hub.

Outside of the start-up wave, progress continues on the National Broadband Network. Its choice of technology direction is as important now as ever, with more Australians logging on and discovering what all the fuss and billions of dollars has been for.

Meanwhile, corporate Australia is seeking to both harness the innovative ideas of the start-up crowd and lead the way in transforming businesses with newfound access to agility and computing power via the cloud.

01.  Daniel Petre and Craig Blair

In September Blair and Petre solidified their status as the country’s most influential investors in the wave of start-up technology companies that promise to grow into new billion-dollar local businesses and fuel the government’s much repeated “jobs and growth” push.

Petre is a former Microsoft executive while Blair is the former managing director of Expedia Australia . They formed AirTree Ventures in 2014, taking just three months to build a $60 million new technology investment fund. This is now spent and AirTree has amassed a new $250 million fund, making it the biggest ever local tech VC.

Alongside other big funds like Blackbird Ventures, Blue Sky Ventures and Square Peg Capital, and some smaller players, they control the future hopes of both entrepreneurs and government for an innovation-led economy.

02. Bill Morrow

A deeply pragmatic operator, Morrow has had a productive year as chief executive of NBN Co. It has launched fibre-to-thenode , hybrid fibre-coaxial and Sky Muster satellite services, despite strident criticism about the limitations of the technology being deployed. As at August, 3 million Australian premises had access to NBN services, with the build due for completion in 2020.

Morrow has sanctioned trials of alternative technology options, which many hope will provide performance closer to the fibre-to-the-premises network initially planned by Labor. His decisions, taken this year, about how to proceed have set in motion events that will determine both the ongoing legacy of Prime Minister Turnbull, who appointed him personally when he was communications minister , and the ability of small and medium-sized businesses to fully participate in the global digital economy.

03. Mike Cannon- Brookes

The successful Nasdaq IPO of Australian technology firm Atlassian secured the reputation of its founders and co-chief executives Mike Cannon- Brookes and Scott Farquhar as the leaders of an emerging generation of entrepreneurs.

On top of running an $8.4 billion public company together, the humble pair are in hot demand in the media, conference and government arenas.

Cannon-Brookes in particular is an increasingly strident voice in the political and business debate about how to best set up the Australian technology ecosystem for future success.

An unsuccessful bid by him and partner Walker Corporation to buy the Australian Technology Park in Sydney to set up a tech industry hub was followed in May by a prominent role backing new industry group TechSydney, which has plans to create a world-leading tech centre.

04. Maile Carnegie

From 2013 until July this year Carnegie was head of Google in Australia, which she steered as it cut through the advertising revenues of media companies.

She then made the surprise move to ANZ Banking Group in the newly created role of group executive for digital banking.

Far from losing power as a result of leaving Google, she is now the highest profile digital executive at an organisation with one of the largest tech budgets in the region – a bank which is desperate to outdo rivals like Commonwealth Bank of Australia in the innovation stakes. Carnegie reports to ANZ chief executive Shayne Elliott , who after taking the bank’s reins in January hired Carnegie to run digital projects, innovation and strategic relationships with a nascent fintech sector that is seeking to challenge the power of the big four banks. ANZ insiders – and those outside seeking to win its business – listen when Carnegie speaks.

05. Dave Curran

Westpac’s chief information officer has a big IT budget, which makes him a key person for tech companies to know. But he also leads a team that is transforming how technology is delivered within Westpac, and pioneering work in areas that will reshape banking. These include the use of blockchain technology, data analytics and early forays into more intelligent automation.

Curran is leading a charge among rivals who see threats and opportunities as giants like Apple enter financial services.

EducationWords ● TIM DODD

Power is in flux in education, which is waiting for the next big idea after the failure of the last two attempts at sweeping reform. Labor’s Gonski school funding reform was halted by the Abbott government. And Abbott’s attempt to deregulate universities was thwarted by Labor, the Greens and independent senators.

What’s next? It’s not clear that the Turnbull government, weakened by its hair’s breadth election win and facing a fractious Senate, will have the stomach to reach for any major reform. That’s why federal Education Minister Simon Birmingham, nominally the most powerful person in education, doesn’t head this year’s list.

However, our schools, which are dropping on international comparison measures, need improvement and it’s the small, relatively cheap changes advocated by researchers such as John Hattie that are winning the battle of ideas.

In education, as in every field, money speaks loudly.

No one brings in more than international students and they have an outsized influence on how Australian universities structure courses and build facilities. Similarly, big philanthropists led by the Australian National University’s $200 million benefactor, funds manager Graham Tuckwell, hold increasing sway.

01. John Hattie

His research as an education professor at the University of Melbourne brings big data to the problem of deciding which are the best, most cost-effective ways of improving schools. His findings are based on statistical meta-analysis of thousands of research papers and his conclusions are the opposite of what many parents expect.

Sample: regular homework is not essential. Hattie is highly influential in policy circles and is becoming better known to the public after being highlighted in The Australian Financial Review and the recent ABC-TV documentary Revolution School .

Governments welcome his research because it says there are ways to improve schools without spending extra money.

02. International students

More than $5 billion a year in tuition fees paid by international students keeps Australia’s universities afloat. It’s nearly as much as the $7 billion a year universities receive in course subsidies from the federal government. Even better for university earnings, half of international students study in business faculties where they pay high fees for courses that are cheap to run. Without international students, universities’ research programs would collapse. Less than one-third of the $10 billion universities spend on research each year comes from government grants.

03. Graham and Louise Tuckwell

The Jersey-based funds manager and his wife shot to the top of the list of Australia’s big education donors in July with a $100 million gift to ANU to invest in new student accommodation halls. The returns will boost a scholarship scheme they started in 2013 with an earlier $50 million donation. Each year the scheme funds 25 promising students for their entire undergraduate course. Many other donors have also given tens of millions of dollars each to universities, including iron ore magnate Andrew Forrest who has promised $65 million to institutions in Western Australia.

04. Simon Birmingham

The federal Education Minister makes the list because of his potential to make change, but he’s hampered by a tight budget and an obstructionist Senate. In schools his challenge is to demonstrate that his preferred low-cost changes – such as minimum literacy and numeracy standards for new teachers and national testing of year 1 kids to identify those who need help – improve Australia’s declining  

school performance. In higher education he’s finding it tough to fulfil his wish to give universities more financial autonomy through limited fee deregulation, which he hopes will ease the pain of a planned 20 per cent cut to course funding.

05. Adrian Piccoli

The NSW Education Minister has used his power decisively and in a surprising way for a National Party politician. He backs the Gonski school funding reforms, walking the talk while his counterparts in Labor states pay them lip service. NSW is the state that adheres most to the Gonski principle of distributing school funding according to each school’s need. Furthermore, his department’s Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation, as a matter of course, analyses data on what works and what doesn’t work in NSW schools. Unfortunately, that is unusual among Australian state education departments.  

PropertyWords ● ROBERT HARLEY

As the property boom rolls on wealth in the industry grows; so too does concern about an end-of-boom reckoning.

Among the big beneficiaries of the extended good times have been Frank Lowy and his family, the value of whose investments in Westfield Corp and Scentre Group have soared since the empire was split in 2014 . For the first time Lowy is not on this list because at 85, though still chairman of the internationally focused Westfield Corp, he has stepped down from all formal roles in Australian property.

His place is hard to fi ll. The industry is well supplied with ambitious billionaires, from James Packer and John Gandel to Lang Walker and China’s richest man, Wanda founder Wang Jianlin, as well as powerful chief executives.

But ultimately it’s a very diffuse sector. The real levers of property are in the hands of the bankers, the regulators and the state and local government planners.  

01. Steve McCann

The Lendlease chief executive has taken his group back to the pinnacle of Australian property with interests that ripple out from Sydney’s Barangaroo to include new office towers, thousands of new homes and retirement units, and some of the nation’s largest infrastructure projects, such as the $2.6 billion twin tunnels on Sydney’s NorthConnex . Of course no one wins them all and Lendlease looks to have missed out on bids for the development of Sydney’s Central Barangaroo and White Bay Power Station .

02. Harry Triguboff

Australia’s richest man, who is the founder and chairman of Meriton, is riding the apartment boom in Sydney, Brisbane and the Gold Coast. This year he launched his largest project ever, the 3000-unit Pagewood Green in Sydney’s east. At 83 , he is still lobbying hard on issues from foreign investment to the folly of voluntary planning agreements with local government.

03. Peter Allen

The Scentre Group chief executive has taken the reins of the local Westfield empire in a role that touches more than 11,600 retail outlets and nearly 100,000 investors. With the support of the Lowy family, he is refining the portfolio, selling non-core assets and boosting the flagship malls with redevelopment, new technology and, in the case of Westfield Sydney, the purchase of the David Jones Market Street store.

Allen is also taking a broader industry role as chairman of peak body the Shopping Centre Council of Australia.

04. Peter Davidson

The head of Property Securities at BT Investment Management, Davidson has emerged as a kingmaker in the Real Estate Investment Trust sector. He ensured the success of the Westfield reconstruction in 2014 with a dramatic intervention at the shareholders’ meeting and this year he strongly, and successfully, opposed the takeover of the Investa Office Fund. Davidson’s is the voice investment bankers want onside as they plan their next raid or raising.

05. Lucy Turnbull

The inaugural chief commissioner of the Greater Sydney Commission has a metropolitan-wide planning responsibility to co-ordinate the NSW government’s economic, infrastructure and housing ambitions with the aspirations of local government and residents.

The commission’s powers extend from the broad to the detailed – backed by the Baird government – and with her own connections in Canberra, Turnbull has a rare opportunity to shape Australia’s international city. Later this year, when the commission releases its first real proposals, the extent of Turnbull’s ambition will become more clear.  

SportWords ● JOHN STENSHOLT

With the four football codes, cricket and tennis earning a combined $1.5 billion in revenue each year, elite sport does not have an issue attracting money. But, as Australian Football League chief executive Gillon McLachlan is fond of saying when describing his sport, while there’s not a revenue problem, there is a spending problem. This encapsulates the difficulty for the nation’s top sports administrators in wielding their power.

Only 17 of Australia’s 49 professional football teams were profitable last year.

McLachlan and Todd Greenberg, his counterpart at the National Rugby League, are grappling with how billion-dollar broadcast deals can help them shore up the financial futures of their respective groups of clubs.

They face challenges at every turn. Fierce opposition from some clubs has already forced McLachlan to dilute luxury tax measures levied on wealthy clubs designed to redistribute money to poorer teams, while Greenberg has been at loggerheads with his clubs regarding how much money will be dispersed across the competition.

Meanwhile, a power struggle is unfolding after the Rio Olympics, with Australian Olympic Committee president John Coates going head-to-head with John Wylie, his counterpart at the Australian Sports Commission, over how funds are spent on elite sport.

The ASC’s power base is being challenged after a disappointing Rio games in which Australia missed its optimistic target of a top-five finish on the medal tally. A lot of money goes into elite sport via federal funding yet there are always cries for more.

01. Gillon McLachlan

A huge broadcast deal has helped make the AFL by far the wealthiest sport in the country.

That makes its chief executive the most powerful sports boss.

He tends to wield it behind the scenes and seeks consensus from the AFL’s 18 clubs when it comes to making big decisions.

But getting demanding club bosses to agree on anything, especially where funds from the competition’s new $2.05 billion TV deal get spent, is a tough job.

McLachlan was criticised for his slow reaction to the Adam Goodes racism row last year but in August moved quickly to call the throwing of a banana at Indigenous Adelaide Crows player Eddie Betts during a match a racist act.

02. John Coates

The International Olympic Committee vice-president was part of the group that controversially allowed some Russian athletes to compete in the Rio Olympics even after evidence of systematic doping in some Russian sports. The most powerful Australian sports administrator on the global stage was outspoken in his concerns about the organisation of Rio.

He heads the IOC efforts to organise the next summer games in Tokyo in 2020. Coates has the ear of government and is throwing his weight around by criticising the Australian Sports Commission’s strategy for divvying up funds between sports. Some say it’s time that Coates, who’s been in the AOC job since 1990, moved on.

03. John Wylie

As chairman of the Australian Sports Commission, Wylie will oversee reviews to find out what went wrong in Rio, following a disappointing medal tally, and to decide where the federal government’s $170 million in elite sports funding should be spent henceforth. The financial carve-up for this year’s Olympics was made via the ASC’s controversial Winning Edge program, which shovelled money into the sports considered to have the best medal chances.

That didn’t work out so well. As a result, Wylie’s power base is under attack from critics, chief among them Coates.

04. James Sutherland

After 15 years as the boss of Cricket Australia, Sutherland’s position at the peak of Australia’s most popular summer sport is firmly entrenched. He’s led the transformation of an organisation once considered one of the most conservative into one that has a colourful Big Bash League attracting its own big crowds and TV ratings. He’s also responsible for one of Australian sport’s best digital businesses, covering cricket as a news organisation and streaming highlights and live coverage for subscribers. Next comes big broadcast deals with Indian TV and, soon, the Australian market. Cricket is a sport that all Australian broadcasters are interested in.

05. Todd Greenberg

The new National Rugby League boss got his baptism of fi re in the form of the Parramatta salary cap scandal, in which breaches back to 2013 were uncovered. Appointed in March, Greenberg saw off legal action and penalised Parramatta. But he has to deal with some powerful vested interests at club level. Getting more corporate support for league would help. ●

HEADLINE: CONNECTING WITH GENERATION CONNECTED
TEXT:
Disaffected and disengaged; that’s the mainstream political view of Millennials. But as activist movements have shown, they don’t have to be. Tap the issues they care about – and use their medium of choice, the internet – and it’s a very different story.

For more than a century Australians have defined themselves along ideological lines, voting for parties on the left or the right on the political spectrum. Then along came the Millennials, who gave that notion a two-finger salute.

Millennials, the generation born between 1980 and 2000, who grew up with the internet and came of age in a world of Google, Wikipedia and social media, have by and large eschewed identifying with any one political party the way their parents or grandparents did. This generation, which has experienced an explosion in information and choices, consumes differently from previous generations, and this applies to how they engage with politics. Broadly speaking, Millennials display little brand loyalty in what they consume, whether it be a pair of jeans, trainers, news or politics.

Twenty years ago a consumer would have visited a nearby shop to buy a pair of trainers. Nowadays, they can go online where there are tens of thousands of trainers to choose from.

It means that Millennials don’t feel fixed in the economic marketplace – and the same holds true for the political sphere.

Mark Textor, co-founder and managing director of CT Group, which has consulted to every federal Coalition election campaign since 1996, has observed these behavioural changes. He warns political parties to be careful and respectful of how they engage with this generation, who now account for one-third of Australian voters, or risk becoming irrelevant. By 2025, Millennials will make up 75 per cent of Australia’s workforce.

“More and more of this generation churn through products in a mercenary fashion. If they’ve got an iPhone and something seeming better comes along it’s simply traded in, there’s generally little loyalty,” says Textor. “That has profound implications for political parties and incumbent governments, regardless of performance. These people want something new and more often than previously.”

Some would argue the shift away from mainstream political parties is already under way. Millennials appear to be seeking a more participatory democracy, centred on the people, and seem less interested in a system where voting Labor or Liberal barely changes the government’s social and economic policies.

“There’s a push for issue-based voting, particularly among younger voters, who are fed up with the existing two-party system,” says Professor Axel Bruns, from the Queensland University of Technology. The push away from party politics is also being driven by a view that the parties are more or less the same. “There’s a sense neither is fully delivering what voters want so there’s less loyalty.”

The internet has enabled hundreds of thousands of people to find alternative ways of organising not just society but the economy; witness the birth and meteoric growth of companies from Uber and Amazon to Airbnb. It’s inevitable that it would also change politics. Activist movements from GetUp! and 350.org to Change.org use the internet and social media effectively to connect with otherwise disparate individuals.

They then galvanise them around issues or an agenda, so as a body appear cohesive, directional and aspirational.

Dominique Fisher, a company director and member of The Australian Financial Review Magazine’s 2016 Power panel, believes such activist groups have stolen the agenda from political parties “who don’t seem to be confident enough to articulate a position other than one straight down the middle … [Political parties] are going to have to work out who they are in relation to young people, pretty rapidly.”

In the July federal election GetUp! spent almost $3 million campaigning on issues its 1 million members are focused on: climate change, better funding for the nation’s hospitals and schools, same-sex marriage and asylum seekers. It raised its war chest from 36,155 donations that averaged $81 each.

As activist groups have grown in number and size, they’ve sucked away money that traditionally might have been donated to the mainstream political parties. While some question the numbers of the GetUp! membership base, it’s worth comparing it with Labor’s 60,000 members or the Liberal’s 80,000.

“They’re getting money from young people who don’t want to give to the big parties,” says Tony Mitchelmore, a former Labor campaign strategist who runs qualitative research and campaign strategy firm Visibility. GetUp! says its donations come from voters of all ages, not just Millennials.

In the federal election, GetUp! did something it has never done before. It campaigned directly against a handful of farright Coalition politicians in their seats, whose positions were contrary to those of its members. While GetUp! didn’t field candidates, it handed out how-to-vote cards suggesting who to put at the top of the ticket, namely those in each electorate aligned most closely with the organisation’s policy positions.

“Here were a small group of people who represented a minority view exercising absolute power over where our Parliament goes in terms of those issues,” says Paul Oosting, GetUp!’s national director. “We targeted them with the explicit intention of unseating them from Parliament. We wanted to show if you hold these views that people power can and will be exercised, and you will be held to account at the ballot box.”

The effect of its campaigning was visible in at least five seats that GetUp! focused on, including that of Andrew Nikolic, one of former prime minister Tony Abbott’s biggest supporters, who lost the seat of Bass in Tasmania. GetUp! tailored its messages in each seat; in Nikolic’s case the lightning rod was the under-resourcing of Launceston General Hospital. Among other MPs targeted were George Christensen, who kept his seat but suffered a 4.3 per cent swing, and Immigration Minister Peter Dutton, who experienced a 5 per cent swing against him, making his seat marginal. “There’s been a growing frustration with the lack of engagement and lack of transparent representation in mainstream politics,” says Oosting. “The youth in particular are really expecting more.

It’s not just a phenomenon constrained to politics as people seek to have more say over the goods they choose.”

People power activist movements such as Podemos in Spain have become political parties but Oosting says that’s not GetUp!’s plan. The organisation is not politically aligned although its campaigning in the past election benefited Labor. It’s why it draws comments such as the following from former Coalition industry minister Ian Macfarlane, who was on the Power panel: “The activist movements will play a bigger and bigger role. I’m not sure we in the Coalition have got our counter to GetUp! but by geez we’re going to have to find it.”

Oosting says GetUp! members already have their sights set on the next federal election. “Our mission now is to scale our movement,” he says. “We made tens of thousands of calls at this recent election and had a huge impact in probably five lower house seats. We want to mobilise it to 10 times the scale at the next election so we can have a bigger impact in the House of Representatives and in the Senate, where things are going in a direction we are really concerned about in relation to the rise of the populist right.”

A survey by JWS Research done after the election and before Parliament resumed indicated that people are giving up on mainstream politicians. The survey supported GetUp!’s arguments that hospitals and health, education and the economy are priority issues on which voters want the government to focus. Yet such issues continue to record the greatest performance gaps for government. For example, 79 per cent of those surveyed rated healthcare as a priority, yet only 17 per cent rated the government as doing a good job in this area.

Another example of how people power can change government policy is that of a petition put on Change.org earlier this year by 16-year-old Chloe Scott, who lives on a dairy farm. She got more than 160,000 signatures to a petition calling for Deputy Prime Minister Barnaby Joyce to act on the massive cut to milk prices that was undermining the dairy farming industry’s welfare. There was already pressure on the government to address this issue but Scott’s online activism added to it. The government responded with a $579 million support package after milk prices were slashed by processors Fonterra and Murray Goulburn .

“That to me is influence and power,” says Fisher. “The concept of collective power. The way people use Instagram and Facebook and other forms of online media to actually shift the tide on policy.”

It’s worth remembering that while Millennials have come together around issue-based politics, it’s not a brand new phenomenon. People who felt forced out of the parliamentary system because they believed it didn’t represent their views have long found a way to have their voices heard. “In the ’60s or ’70s it used to be called an extra-parliamentary opposition, a form of opposition outside of Parliament when nobody in Parliament represented your views on a critical issue,” says Bruns, pointing to protests over issues from the Vietnam War to women’s rights.

The warning that the major parties need to work out how to engage with young people or risk irrelevancy is timely, given the rise in the independent vote in both the upper and lower houses in recent elections. But while many Millennials are disaffected, they’re arguably persuadable – if they can be shown there’s space for them to make government into a representative force.

George Wright ran Labor’s slick 2016 federal election campaign, which brought the party closer to winning than anyone expected. Through its online messaging, he says, Labor encouraged 20,000 young Australians to enrol to vote.

“All voters are important and in many ways young voters are no different from other voters,” Wright says. “They will respond to politics which is relevant to them and meaningful to their lives, values and aspirations. What you need to communicate and campaign effectively with young voters are the same things you need for everyone else – a relevant message that gets through.

“You just have to work a bit harder with young voters.

They are a bit harder to listen to through the traditional tools of political campaigning – polling and focus groups – so you need to go elsewhere to find out more about what they think: online, listening, asking and engagement are the key here.

“And once you have a relevant message, young voters can again be a bit harder to get to using the traditional mainstream broadcast communications tools of politics. We relied almost exclusively on narrow-cast, highly individualised and targeted online communications and lots of direct and face-to-face campaigning for our younger voter campaigns. You can campaign effectively with and to younger voters. I just think mainstream politics often ignores younger voters on issues and on communications and then wonders why and complains about the fact they appear disengaged. If you want results – get serious.”

Dion Appel , who runs DDB Lifelounge , which researches Millennials, agrees. “Political parties need to segment their messages so topical issues can be prioritised to the younger demographic. This demographic is very well informed and extremely savvy in how they consume messaging. They don’t take the lead from Gen X or Baby Boomer parents in the types of political parties they back.”

Then again, perhaps society has changed to such an extent that the political system that has served it so well for so long is out of date. Millennials have used the power of the internet to disrupt every other part of life. Why not politics?

“Nothing is safe from disruption,” says Appel.

Watch this space. ●

HEADLINE: OUT OF THE BOX
TEXT:
Stan Grant has emerged over the past year as a potent new voice on Indigenous affairs. Just don’t assume it’s all he wants to talk about.

N.A: Your second book, Talking to My Country, published this year, is a deeply personal account of your life story as well as your thoughts about race in Australia. What did you hope to achieve by writing it?

S.G: James Baldwin, the great African-American writer, said he wished for nothing more than to be an honest man and a good writer. That was my guiding principle. I wanted to write it as well and as honestly as I could. But it’s only a moment in time, a part of my history, not all of me.

You’re a very private man – how did it feel to tell your story publicly?

It was confronting and also really emotional. It’s a release in a sense, but equally, since the book has come out, I’ve also felt a bit constrained, as if people were projecting things onto me that I don’t want and that I can’t possibly live up to.

Suddenly people want to ask me constantly about Aboriginal affairs, about the Royal Commission [into the Child Protection and Youth Detention Systems of the Northern Territory]. I’m not a lawyer, I don’t live in the Territory, and I don’t presume to have answers to all of that.

In a way, speaking out about Indigenous issues has narrowed my life a bit uncomfortably, and I feel like I’m trying to reclaim some of myself.

You’re a journalist who has worked for the Seven Network, SBS, the ABC and Sky in Australia and for CNN in Hong Kong, China and the Middle East. You said in your book that journalism had been your salvation.

What did you mean by that?

It gave my life a meaning and a purpose. I should never have got to where I am today. There were huge gaps in my education – I’d been to more than 12 schools before I was even into my teens. My family was beyond poor. We were homeless, we moved from town to town as my father looked for work. Throughout my childhood, I loved stories and I loved words, and even when I wasn’t going to school I read whatever I could. From the moment I came into journalism I had a home. I’d never really had one before – I didn’t exist comfortably in any world, but I was instinctively good at journalism. It opened up a world to me that I could never even have imagined existing.

Let’s talk about power. You’ve said that a sense of powerlessness haunts your people. What do you mean?

We’re inherently powerless. We’re a people who cannot define ourselves, we cannot determine our destiny independently of a nation that dispossessed us. There are no treaties, there’s no recognition of the fundamental inherent rights of our people. We feel like supplicants in Australia.

When you speak these days, people listen. Your speeches get a lot of publicity. Do you exercise a power of sorts?

No, because there is nothing materially that I can change. I can’t make a law, I can’t mend a broken body or save a kid from going to jail. I don’t defend kids in court. As journalists, our greatest capacity is to be able to shine a light into a world people haven’t seen before, to inspire empathy, to ask the fundamental question, “What if that were me? How would I feel if that were my son or daughter?” That’s what I seek to do, but I don’t see that as being a powerful position.

Earlier this year it seemed you were contemplating a career in politics. How do you feel about that now?

At the time there were so many expectations, and a lot of pressure from people wanting me to go into politics. I needed to try to hold on to who I was and not be swept up in all of that, not give in to the constant massaging of my ego or other people’s expectations. Politics is a business, a calling, and people going into politics need to be politicians first and foremost in the same way that I’m a journalist. So I need to ask myself, ‘Am I that person? Am I going to stand on a street corner and hand out a flyer with my photo on it? Am I going to shake hands at school fetes?’ Essentially, I’m a solitary person. I like to be at home, to read, to think, to write, to play my music, to be around my kids. I don’t need a lot of other people and I don’t need that approval. At the end of the day, when I look at it like that, I think you’re either a poet or a politician, and there’s more of the poet in me than the politician. Poetry and words are about the truth and politics is about the possible. Politics is a worthy calling, it’s a huge sacrifice, it’s where change and law are made, but it’s not me.

Do you think you can exert greater power from outside that realm than you would be able to from within?

Politicians live at the pointy end of power. Peter Garrett has told me that there were things done that would not have been done, had he not been there. That is real power.

The storyteller speaks with permanence rather than power.

That’s why the words of someone like James Baldwin speak to me still. He wrote that, “For the state, a nigger is a nigger is a nigger. Sometimes Mr or Mrs Nigger or Dr Nigger.”

If we hear those words and then we reflect on the fact that black American professors can be pulled over by police on the basis on their colour, that black people in America can be shot by police, that a black American president can have his citizenship questioned, then Baldwin’s words speak to us still.

Just because the best politicians are the best storytellers, doesn’t mean there’s always going to be the best outcome. At the moment, Vladimir Putin is speaking a story to the Russian people that resonates with them. When he speaks about the nostalgia for the Soviet empire, about the power that has been lost, about a strong Russia and then he acts on that, his popularity surges because he is speaking to something that the people believe in.

In China, every political leader who speaks to the Chinese people mentions the 100 years of humiliation by foreign forces, and that speaks to the Chinese sense of identity.

You said in your book that in mid-2012, during your last year working overseas for CNN, you were driven by a fear of being unmasked as a fraud. What did you mean by that?

It was a feeling that what people saw in me and what I projected were not really me, that I could never meet those expectations. I think many journalists have that sense of being a bit fraudulent, that there’s always the risk of being unmasked.

You’ve said that when you were at university, mixing with other Indigenous students, you became politicised for the first time and grew to “hate your white blood”. Do you still feel like that?

Not at all. The fact that there’s white blood in me speaks to the history of my country so I don’t feel ashamed of that. My grandmother – my mother’s mother – was a white woman who lived with an Aboriginal man and had Aboriginal children so I could never feel ashamed of her.

When I started university, I gained a new vocabulary that helped me to make sense of what I felt instinctively. When you face the realities of our country’s history in a formal way it’s confronting, and in my early days of university my feelings hardened into a strong sense of resentment about what had happened to my people. But I’ve grown beyond that. If I were the same person now that I was then, I would never have experienced the things that I have. Tracy, my wife, is white. I don’t have any hatred for white people, but part of my journey was to try to make sense of it all.

In a speech you gave in late July, shortly after the revelations about juvenile detention in the Northern Territory, you said that Australia needed a treaty with its Indigenous people and a truth and reconciliation commission. Previously you thought they might be too divisive. What changed your mind?

I’ve always believed that we need a treaty but I’m aware of the politics, and right now we’re struggling even to get traction on recognition. A treaty isn’t even on the agenda. Of course Aboriginal people want a treaty that recognises our inherent sovereign rights, as other countries have. As for a truth and reconciliation commission, if I’ve been guilty of anything in the past it’s been trying to be too diplomatic.

Having lived away from Australia for a long time, it’s clear to me now that we need to hold a mirror up to ourselves because Aboriginal people cannot be free of the chains of our history until it’s acknowledged and spoken about. A truth and reconciliation commission might well be a cathartic moment. South Africa has had one, as has Canada.

You’ve been accused of having a nostalgia for injustice.

What’s your response to that?

You can’t have a nostalgia for something that’s not in the past. This is a lived experience. Why are the first peoples of Australia the most jailed? Why are we crippled by unemployment, and by poor outcomes in health, housing and education? How can you possibly say that this is not connected to our history? It is born of neglect and exclusion and still today Aboriginal people are denied the rights that exist for Indigenous people in other parts of the world.

This idea of a nostalgia for injustice is ludicrous, and it’s offensive. There is no way anyone would say that Jewish people have a nostalgia for injustice because they say ‘Never again’. When Australians visit the fields of France and the shores of Gallipoli, do they have a nostalgia for suffering and misery? It’s only Aboriginal people who are accused of this nostalgia. Others can celebrate but we have to forget.

When you returned to Australia in late 2012 after more than a decade overseas you said you felt adrift, that you were looking for a sense of purpose. Have you found one?

When I first returned I was wondering what my role was here, as a reporter. Then I stumbled almost accidentally into writing about the Adam Goodes booing incident for Guardian Australia, then giving the speech on racism, then writing my book. These have given me a sense of purpose but I’m also feeling a bit suffocated by that. I don’t necessarily want to carry that burden of responsibility.

Aboriginal people are put in a box and the struggle for me as an Aboriginal man is to live outside that box – not to be what other Aboriginal people want me to be, what my family want me to be, what Australia wants or expects. I was never an Aboriginal journalist, I was always just a journalist and I want to be judged on my merits. I feel right now that the box that I’ve tried to avoid is starting to hold me in and I don’t like the feeling.

Is there a trade-off though, that you can introduce important issues into public debate?

No, it’s not a trade-off. If I want to speak about Aboriginal issues, I will. But I don’t want to be put in that box, I want to talk about other things. If someone wants to talk to me about China, where I spent seven to eight years of my life, or about the Middle East, or Afghanistan or Pakistan, I’m equally interested and I have a lot of experience and expertise in those areas. Surely we need to get to a stage where an Aboriginal person can be a Nobel-prize-winning physicist, or secretary-general of the United Nations, or an expert in Greek antiquity or Roman history in the same way that everybody else can. It is so important that we don’t keep being put back into that box. That, if anything, has been the guiding principle of my life. ●

Stan Grant spoke to The Australian Financial Review Magazine at the Byron Writers Festival. This is an edited extract of that conversation.

Talking to My Country was published by HarperCollins in March.

HEADLINE: NO WE COULDN'T
TEXT:
Few presidents take office wrapped in as many hopes and dreams as Barack Obama did, both his own and those of his people. How did a leader so determined to unite Americans end up presiding over one of the most divisive times in US political history?

Not long before a vibrant and optimistic Barack Obama was elected president of the United States, he pledged to “turn the page on the ugly partisanship in Washington, so we can bring Democrats and Republicans together to pass an agenda that works for the American people”.

Obama moved into the White House seemingly believing he could transcend entrenched political hostilities and bridge divides to pursue a common purpose. The Democrat arrived in January 2009 as the first African-American president, a historic milestone that in some ways affirmed one of the founding principles of America, that “all men are created equal”. It was a hugely significant moment, especially for black Americans. Not surprisingly, many of Obama’s fellow Americans latched onto his perhaps naive hope of ushering in a new era of bipartisan achievement.

Nearly eight years on, in the final year of a presidency that formally finishes in January, Obama acknowledged that his hope for co-operation had been found wanting.

“It’s one of the few regrets of my presidency: that the rancour and suspicion between the parties has gotten worse instead of better,” he said in his final state of the union address in January.

“I have no doubt a president with the gifts of Lincoln or Roosevelt might have better bridged the divide, and I guarantee I’ll keep trying to be better so long as I hold this office.”

As difficult as it is for those who warm to Obama to fathom, by one measure he’ll exit office on a par with George W. Bush as the most divisive US president in modern history.

Bush’s invasion of Iraq in 2003, which led to thousands of American deaths and trillions of dollars being spent, badly divided American conservatives and liberals.

The measure in question was created by Gary Jacobson, professor of political science at the University of California San Diego. Author of a book about the second Bush presidency, A Divider, Not a Uniter, Jacobson calculates divisiveness by measuring the proportion of voters for the president’s party who believe he did a good job (about 80 to 85 per cent of Democrats for Obama and the same of Republicans for George W. Bush) and subtracting the share of voters from the opposition party who think he did a good job (about 10 per cent for both presidents). “He is as polarising as Bush was,” says Jacobson of Obama.

David Brady, professor of political economy at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, says Obama “set an impossibly high standard for himself”. A contributing author of the 2006 book Red and Blue Nation? Characteristics and Causes of America’s Polarized Politics, Brady says “the expectations were so high, he never could have lived up to them. There’s governing and campaigning. In my view, he was one of the best campaigners and overestimated his ability to govern.”

The political rifts during Obama’s tenure are exemplified by the 17-day government shutdown in 2013, as Republicans tried to unpick the president’s signature healthcare insurance expansion; a near sovereign debt default after an impasse over the country’s debt ceiling; the passage of only one annual budget in eight years; and the failure to agree on issues even where there was common ground, including immigration, infrastructure investment and corporate tax reform.

On gun control, despite a rolling wave of mass shootings, an anguished Obama – like presidents before him – has been unable to implement even modest reforms such as tighter background checks for weapon buyers, stopping people on terrorism watch lists from acquiring firearms and limiting access to high-powered automatic guns. The blame can’t be sheeted home to him though. Republicans, beholden to the powerful National Rifle Association, have stood in his way at every turn, putting the US out of step with the Western world.

On the plus side, Obama will be remembered for significantly expanding healthcare insurance for the poor and middle class; rescuing the financial system from the 2008 financial crisis; recalibrating American foreign policy away from military adventurism and putting more onus on other countries to contribute; and leading international climate change co-operation.

His presidency might not have been as revolutionary as the left had dared to dream, and it might have suffered constant Republican roadblocks on economic and social policy, but it was far-reaching. Among other things, Obama restored dignity to the Oval Office, which had been tarnished by Bush’s disastrous Iraq war and before that, the sex scandals of Bill Clinton. Obama injected humanity and glamour back into the White House, too, by virtue of perhaps the most photogenic and one of the most-loved first families since the Camelot days of John F. Kennedy.

The good looks, cool personas and senses of humour of both President Obama and his wife Michelle made them popular with young Americans and those traditionally less engaged in politics. Goofing about on late night TV to promote his healthcare reforms; conducting hilarious stand-up skits at the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner; and chatting with Jerry Seinfeld while driving around in a 1963 blue Corvette for Seinfeld’s Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee showed Obama to be a dab hand at soft diplomacy.

So too, the First Lady, who in 2013 danced alongside host Jimmy Fallon on The Tonight Show to encourage parents to get moving with their kids, and more recently had her own spin in a car with rapper Missy Elliott for James Corden’s popular Carpool Karaoke.

The senator from Illinois inherited a dire state of affairs when he took over in January 2009. The economy was losing 800,000 jobs a month as Wall Street teetered on the brink of collapse, and America remained bogged down in costly wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Patently, Obama was dealt a dud hand. Still, presidents don’t have the luxury of selecting the environment over which they preside; they’re judged on how they respond to circumstances.

Promisingly, the handover from the outgoing Bush administration was smooth and professional as, in the midst of the Great Recession, both sides focused on putting “Team America” first. The bipartisanship didn’t last long, however, once Obama had to deal with Republicans in Congress.

Republican leaders were vowing to block the new president’s ambitious agenda even before he was sworn in. Not only did they vehemently disagree with his leftist policies on healthcare, climate change, taxes, business regulation and gay marriage – and his stance on most other key issues – they also believed their best chance of wrecking his presidency was to oppose nearly anything of substance that he attempted to implement.

“Republican elites’ strategy in dealing with him was to go into full-scale opposition,” says Gary Jacobson.

In a 2012 article entitled “The Party of No”, Time magazine revealed that in late 2008 and early 2009 then-House Republican whip Eric Cantor and then-Senate minority leader Mitch McConnell orchestrated secret meetings about how to best obstruct Obama. Reporter Michael Grunwald quoted former Ohio senator George Voinovich on the state of play: “If he was for it, we had to be against it.”

Despite such co-ordinated defiance, Democrats controlled the House and Senate in Obama’s first two years, so as the economy nosedived in early 2009 Obama was able to push through the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. A $US831 billion package designed to save jobs and prop up the economy was followed by government bailouts of the banking and automobile industries.

Though left-wing and conservative economists are at odds on the efficacy of the rescue package, most agree that without it, unemployment would have risen above the realised 10 per cent peak and the economic contraction would have been deeper. Inside the Obama administration there’s a strongly held conviction that he got this big call right, even though the economic recovery has been painfully slow.

Annual economic growth averaged about 1.5 per cent during Obama’s first seven years to the end of 2015, half of the 3 per cent yearly average for 1980 through to 2008. Even stripping out the deep 2.8 per cent shrinkage in Obama’s first year – when the economy was on a preset course from the Bush era – annual GDP has averaged a mediocre 2.1 per cent.

More positively, unemployment dipped below 5 per cent in early 2016, albeit helped by a slump in the workforce participation rate to a near 40-year low as baby boomers retire and the long term unemployed stop looking for work.

Middle-class wages growth has been subdued, continuing a trend that started three decades ago. But in a sign the tide may finally be turning, Census Bureau figures published in September showed the median household income rose for the first time in Obama’s tenure, leaping 5.2 per cent in 2015 to $US56,500. It is however still 1.6 per cent below the 2007 level. The share of people in the US living in poverty dropped to 13.5 per cent in 2015, one of the biggest declines in decades.

Fiscally, the budget deficit has plunged from 10.8 per cent of GDP in 2009 to about 2.5 per cent, though net federal public debt is nearly $US14 trillion – a relatively high 75 per cent of GDP. On Wall Street, the sharemarket has nearly tripled, providing a boon for the wealthy. Yet many ordinary Americans feel they’re not sharing in the spoils. Nearly a third of respondents to a 2015 Federal Reserve household survey, representing nearly 76 millions adults, reported struggling to get by or just getting by.

Betsey Stevenson, a former White House economic adviser to President Obama, suspects that over time it will become more evident just how well he handled the financial crisis.

“As economists continue to study this, Obama will look better than the public gave him credit for during his presidency,” Stevenson says. “It’s not clear we could have grown faster out of a financial crisis.”

International comparisons suggest she has a point. Despite Wall Street being at the epicentre of the global financial crisis, the long-term damage in many other economies has been far worse. According to National Bureau of Economic Research economist Laurence Ball, between December 2007 and 2015 the recession wiped an estimated 4.7 per cent off US potential economic output relative to the pre-crisis growth path.

Twenty-three OECD countries lost a weighted average of 8.4 per cent long-term GDP over the same period. The US was fourth-best off, behind Switzerland, Germany and a commodities-fuelled Australia. Today, the US economy and its banks are in far better shape than those in Europe.

Obama’s other big early achievement was his healthcare insurance package. In March 2010, the Affordable Care Act passed Congress without a single Republican vote. Dubbed Obamacare, the signature policy extended a mix of public and employer-provided healthcare insurance to about 18 million Americans and banned insurers from denying coverage to patients with pre-existing conditions. It’s estimated the package will cost the US government $US 1.35 trillion over 10 years, about 5 per cent of the health budget.

Signing the legislation, Obama said it reflected “the core principle that everybody should have some basic security when it comes to their healthcare”. Certainly, it went some way towards reducing the healthcare gap between the rich and poor. A study by the New York Federal Reserve found that the expansion of healthcare cover “increased protection against financial hardship” for low-income individuals and families.

But it hasn’t solved all the country’s health problems. By international standards healthcare spending is much higher in the US but overall health outcomes are inferior. Unlike in Australia, Britain and Canada, public coverage of patients remains limited, a symptom of the American right-wing stance against government-funded healthcare.

Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders campaigned this year for the kind of universal, publicly funded system that operates in many other countries. It struck a chord with many but he lost the race to Hillary Clinton. Henry Aaron , an economics fellow at the Brookings Institution , says it’s still too early to tell if Obamacare will fulfill its goal of controlling health spending growth over the longer term.

To small-government Republicans, Obamacare represented a treacherous government takeover of the healthcare system (even though it maintained private hospitals and insurers).

They were infuriated among other things by tax penalties to be levied on certain employers who failed to offer insurance.

Obama used up tremendous political capital early in his reign to pass the stimulus package and shake up the healthcare system. Republican Senator David Perdue , a former chief executive of Reebok and Dollar General , blames Obama’s heavy-handed regulation of healthcare and banks for the lack of co-operation by his side of politics, while acknowledging that Congress is not working effectively.

“In business you have to have a sense of urgency,” says Perdue, who took office in January 2015. “Unfortunately, in the Senate and the House there is a lack of sense of urgency and priorities.” Both those chambers are controlled by his own conservative party.

A common criticism from Republicans is that Obama failed to reach across the aisle, that he didn’t “buddy up” by inviting conservatives to play golf or share a nightcap at the White House. “Aloof” and “professorial” are two words Republicans use to disparage the former University of Chicago Law School professor . Some Democrats in Congress, too, were frustrated by his lack of engagement to help negotiate and steer through legislation. Jim Manley , a former spokesman for Democratic Senate leader Harry Reid , told Bloomberg in 2014 that “Obama doesn’t like to get his hands dirty” and “floats above it all”.

It didn’t take long for the disdain of Republican lawmakers to transmit to the conservative rank and file, many of whom were already down due to the financial crisis hangover.

Democrats suffered devastating losses in the November 2010 midterm elections, in which Republicans gained 63 seats in the House to recapture a majority in the biggest thrashing since the 1940s. As the Tea Party uprising took hold, Republicans picked up six seats in the Senate to chip away at the Democratic majority. Fiscal and social conservatives such as Ted Cruz, ringleader of the government shutdown, were elected pledging not to compromise with Obama.

Given the hostility of Republicans towards Obama and his agenda, it’s doubtful that a more collaborative president would have enjoyed greater success. “As far as I’m concerned, the politics in this system right now are broken,” Manley says.

“It is just a partisan killing field these days.”

Had Obama been more consultative, he would likely have still found it difficult to convince Republicans to compromise, given their hardline, obstructionist attitude. “I think anything he did that was in line with what his party wanted to do would have been resisted by Republicans,” says Gary Jacobson.

Robert Weiner, a former adviser to president Clinton in the 1990s, sums up the climate. “Politics is very different now in terms of what you can get done than it was in a bipartisan era.”

Former adviser Stevenson says Obama was totally open to negotiation and compromise but was never given the chance by conservatives. “Obama is one of the most reasonable people I ever met and completely comfortable with trade-offs to meet people in the middle.”

The political polarisation of the US had been increasing since the 1990s – Republicans becoming more conservative on issues such as guns, abortion, gay rights and government intervention in the economy, and Democrats more liberal – but there’s no doubt it surged during the Obama years.

Beginning with the Tea Party insurgence of 2010, the growing polarisation climaxed with the improbable rise of Donald Trump as Republican presidential nominee.

Nearly half of Republican voters believe Obama was born outside the US (he was born in the US state of Hawaii), implying that he’s an illegitimate president. Some think he’s a closet Muslim (he’s a practising Christian).

Republican Party delegate Charlie Wingo from the deeply conservative state of Georgia is indicative of many from his side of politics. At a bar outside the Republican National Convention in July, the 78-year-old refers to Obama not as the president but as the “current occupant of the White House”, calling him “the ultimate public housing inhabitant” and the worst president in history for his “socialisation of medicine”.

Opposition to Obama is often ideological, sometimes racially motivated and often a subtle combination of the two.

Beyond the campaign trail, Obama has rarely sought to be popular when he governs. His decisions appear overwhelmingly driven by what he believes are in the best interests of the US. One of his biggest perceived foreign policy blunders was the failure to follow through on a “red line” threat to Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. “We have been very clear to the Assad regime … that a red line for us is we start seeing a whole bunch of chemical weapons moving around or being utilised,” Obama said in 2012 on the prospect of a US military intervention in the war-torn Middle East nation. “That would change my calculus. That would change my equation.”

A year later, a rebel-controlled neighbourhood of Damascus was attacked with sarin gas, killing 1400 men, women and children. US intelligence had “high confidence” that the Assad regime was responsible. After careful deliberation Obama chose not to punish Assad with air strikes. He copped widespread criticism from the foreign policy establishment that his impotence had dented US credibility and emboldened aggressors such as Russia in eastern Ukraine and China in the South China Sea.

But he remains proud of that decision. “The perception was that my credibility was at stake, that America’s credibility was at stake,” Obama told the The Atlantic for a story published in April 2016. “And so for me to press the pause button at that moment, I knew would cost me politically. And the fact that I was able to pull back from the immediate pressures and think through in my own mind what was in America’s interest, not only with respect to Syria but also with respect to our democracy, was as tough a decision as I’ve made – and I believe ultimately it was the right decision to make.”

Internationally, Obama’s emphasis on diplomacy and economic engagement over military force has been both welcomed and criticised. Retreats – though not entire withdrawals – from the Middle East, plus the Iran nuclear deal, upset allies in Israel and Saudi Arabia. The rise of the terror group Islamic State and his refusal to forcefully confront it via a ground assault in the Middle East has been criticised by foreign policy hawks.

Obama was eager to meet his election pledge to withdraw troops from Iraq and he opposed intervening more in Syria.

The pullback may have created a vacuum for Islamic State to rise, though Bush’s Iraq invasion was how it all started. The killing of terrorist mastermind Osama Bin Laden by US Special Forces in Pakistan in May 2011, a risky operation authorised by Obama, was a significant achievement.

The US pivot to Asia has been cheered by Australia, Japan and most of south-east Asia , though not necessarily by rising rival China. But Obama’s legacy as the Pacific President in Asia may ultimately hinge on whether Congress passes the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal. Presidential candidates Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton have both come out against the pact, in response to claims that trade deals have cost blue-collar manufacturing jobs. If the US fails to ratify the TPP this year, as appears likely, it would be a bitter blow to Obama’s legacy on engagement with Asia.

The Obamas plan to stay in Washington DC after leaving the White House in January, at least until their youngest daughter graduates from high school, making Obama the first president in almost 100 years to remain in the nation’s capital after service. He’s signalled he would like to return to community organising, though undoubtedly on a grander scale than during his student politics days.

“I’ll go back to doing the kind of work that I was doing before, just trying to find ways to help people,” Obama told school students last year. “Help young people get educations, and help people get jobs, and try to bring businesses into neighbourhoods that don’t have enough businesses. That’s the kind of work that I really love to do.”

He will set up his presidential library in Chicago and presumably at some stage begin writing his memoirs, tales that could generate tens of millions of dollars for his retirement fund. He’s ruled out accepting a political office or Supreme Court appointment, and seems more interested in returning to teach law at university.

Obama seems happy enough with the prospect of leaving the Oval Office. According to an amusing account in July by The New York Times, during his darkest hours, when there was one too many decisions to make, Obama used to fantasise with former chief of staff Rahm Emanuel about moving to Hawaii and setting up a beach shack that sold only white, medium-sized T-shirts. The running joke saw Emanuel turn to Obama on testing occasions and simply say, “white”, to which Obama would respond, “medium”.

If Clinton wins the election, she may use Obama as an occasional sounding board. “You know, I’ve already put him on notice,” she said on America’s 60 Minutes program this year. “I’m going to be picking up the phone. I’m going to be calling and asking for his advice.”

While Obama’s record is inextricably intertwined with polarisation, both domestically and internationally, from any reasonable centrist perspective he was a more competent president than his predecessor. The economy is in better shape and foreign policy less gratuitously aggressive. His long-term legacy is yet to be fully felt, and history may remember him kindly. The tragedy of his presidency, however, is that the audacity of hope with which he arrived was overridden by bitter partisan divisions that prevented him from achieving everything he set out to do. ●

Changing times: from the audacity of hope to a bitter partisan divide

November 4, 2008

Senator Barack Obama of Illinois easily defeats Republican Senator John McCain in the presidential election, becoming the first African-American to win the White House.

January 20, 2009

Obama is inaugurated as the 44th president of the United States. An estimated 1.8 million people crowd into Washington DC, making it the largest event in the history of the city.

February 17, 2009

Obama signs the $US831 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act to shield the US economy from the global financial crisis. It passes Congress without any support from Republicans, who prefer tax cuts to additional spending.

March 23, 2010

The Affordable Care Act becomes law, expanding health insurance to millions of Americans.

November 2, 2010

Mid-term elections lead to big gains for Republicans in the so-called “Tea Party wave”. The GOP takes over the House of Representatives and gains seats in the Senate.

May 1, 2011

Obama and his national security team watch from the White House as Osama Bin Laden is killed by US Special Forces in Pakistan.

November 6, 2012

Obama easily defeats Republican challenger Mitt Romney to win re-election.

Democrats hold the Senate and regain some seats in the House of Representatives.

October, 2013

The US government is partially shut down for 17 days when Republicans refuse to approve government spending and try to destroy Obamacare. The US almost defaults on its debt.

Obama accuses Republicans of blackmail, before a divided Republican party relents and votes to reopen the government and lift the debt ceiling.

November 4, 2014

Republicans win huge gains in mid-term elections, seizing control of the Senate and enlarging their majority in the House of Representatives.

June 25, 2015

Obama’s signature legislation, the Affordable Care Act, is upheld by the US Supreme Court.

June 26, 2015 The US Supreme Court supports Obama’s position on gay marriage, legalising it across the nation.

July 14, 2015

Iran and the UN Security Council’s five permanent members, plus Germany and the European Union, agree to a deal that curtails Iran’s nuclear weapons program in return for the lifting of Western sanctions.

October 5, 2015

Agreement is reached between the US, Australia and 10 other Pacific Rim nations on the Trans- Pacific Partnership, a trade deal covering 40 per cent of the world’s economy.

The US Congress still needs to ratify it.

November to December 2015

The Obama administration and China lead other nations at the UN Climate Change Conference to agree to limit greenhouse emissions.

March 20, 2016

Obama visits Cuba, following the re-establishment of diplomatic relations which ends 54 years of isolation.

June 12, 2016

A lone gunman pledging support to Islamic State attacks patrons at Pulse, a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, murdering 49 people.

April 30, 2016

A comical Obama roasts Donald Trump in his final address to the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.

June 9, 2016

Obama endorses Hillary Clinton for president after she seals the Democratic primary race.

July 25 to 27, 2016

Obama warmly embraces Hillary Clinton on stage at the Democratic National Convention. He and wife Michelle deliver rousing speeches.

HEADLINE: R . E . S . P . E . C . T
TEXT:
That’s what Pauline Hanson wants. Will the political mainstream be canny enough to give it to her this time around?

They shuffled into the polling booths. Eyes down. Mostly older white men. They ignored attempts to press voting cards into their hands. Their demeanour marked them as Pauline Hanson’s dispossessed, according to Shayne Neumann, a federal MP who probably knows more about the One Nation leader than anyone outside the party in Parliament.

They knew who they were voting for, and they didn’t care if southern elites called her ignorant, racist or a xenophobe, Neumann says. It made them respect her more. She said what they believed, what no one else would: that Australia was going backwards, economically, socially and culturally. They turned out, in their hundreds of thousands, in Queensland, New South Wales and Western Australia, and upended the balance of power in Australian politics.

Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party, to use its full name, won four Senate seats. That makes Hanson Canberra’s new joint-kingmaker. The government, when opposed by the Greens and Labor, needs nine extra votes to pass laws through the Senate. Liberal Democrat David Leyonhjelm and Family First leader Bob Day are natural allies. That leaves Hanson’s team and Nick Xenophon’s three senators to deliver Malcolm Turnbull a majority, which he can use to drive through the kind of policy changes that could save his prime ministership.

Xenophon is a notorious self-publicist. But he’s also a deal doer. The government knows it can work with him. Hanson is the wildcard. Few people in Canberra know her, let alone how to manage a woman who has spent 20 years in the public eye while being shunned by the political establishment.

Hanson craves legitimacy. Turnbull needs to prove himself.

Together, they could be Canberra’s oddest couple. Former members, opposing politicians and journalists predict One Nation, if handled carefully, could be co-opted to the Coalition agenda. It is Turnbull’s choice: is the investment banker prepared to cut deals with the devil?

“In the first instance there will be chaos and difficult demands,” says David Oldfield, a One Nation co-founder who is no longer involved in the party. “But there is a lot that can be achieved by the government if it negotiates with them.”

Left-wing journalist Margo Kingston, who wrote a 1999 book on Hanson, says the One Nation founder resents her treatment in 1996, when she burst onto the national stage by winning a federal seat on an anti-Aboriginal and anti-Asian platform. Apart from trying to destroy her party through preference swaps, other politicians refused to treat Hanson as a legitimate public figure. Even though a one-term local government councillor and small-businesswoman from Ipswich had created a political movement that won a million votes, Hanson didn’t receive any respect, privately or publicly, from her political peers. That cut.

“She was shunned in ’96,” Kingston says. “That drove her to the hard right. I don’t think she’s a rational actor. She’s an emotional actor.”

Hanson well knows the taste of defeat. At the 1998 election – when One Nation was a powerful rising force – Hanson came first in her seat but was defeated by a Liberal who received Labor preferences. She spent 18 years trying to break back into federal or state politics. There were failed runs in 1998, 2001, 2003, 2004, 2007, 2009 and 2013.

In between running for office, she traded on her fame, appearing on Celebrity Apprentice, Dancing with the Stars, Who Wants to be a Millionaire and This is Your Life. She wrote an autobiography, Untamed and Unashamed.

Finally, her time returned. This year’s double dissolution election made it twice as easy for minor parties to be elected to the Senate. The liberal Turnbull was less popular than the right-wing Tony Abbott among conservative Queenslanders, and no preference swap between Labor and Liberal was going to stop her.

When Hanson arrived at the Senate for her first day, she had a quip ready: “I’m back.” She now wants to be treated as a player. “She has to be accepted and respected as a genuine representative,” Kingston says. “She doesn’t want to blow the place up.”

Nationwide, One Nation got more than 4 per cent of the 2016 vote, an impressive result for an extremist party with no existing parliamentary representation. In Queensland, the party was the first Senate choice of 9 per cent of voters.

One Nation has assembled policies that reflect hostility to the state, minorities and taxation. It wants the federal Family Court replaced, a moratorium on coal-seam gas production, trade tariffs to protect manufacturers, $100 billion in new taxes on foreign companies and lower taxes on average Australian income earners.

“She doesn’t have interaction with ‘normal’ people,” Kingston says. “She’s surrounded by crackpots.”
